title: Quantum Entanglement Information Matrix
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents a unique phenomenon where two or more particles become inextricably linked, regardless of the distance separating them. This interconnectedness has profound implications for information processing and, potentially, for the manipulation of quantum systems. This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement to construct a novel matrix-based system capable of significantly enhancing the prediction capabilities of probabilistic systems. The core claim centers on a matrix structure designed to effectively handle complex non-linear relationships inherent in such systems. We investigate the potential of incorporating quantum entanglement principles, specifically the 'information transmission' mechanism, into a matrix framework to achieve superior prediction accuracy. This work presents a theoretical framework and preliminary investigation of such a matrix, focusing on its ability to address limitations of traditional matrix operations.

Rust Implementation Run from lemur-rs/: cd lemur-rs cargo test cargo run --release --bin lemur -- vectors --tau 3 --signers 2 --slot 0 --msg "artifact check" --out /tmp/lemur-rs-vectors.json cargo run --release --bin lemur -- sizes cargo run --release --bin bench -- --fast cargo run --release --bin bench_aggregate cargo run --release --bin bench_breakdown cargo run --release --bin bench_verify -- --zero-fixture --n 1048576 --reps 1 The Rust CLI mirrors the Python CLI. Benchmarking And Sizes The Python and Rust implementations ship the fixed d=256, k=4, tau=20, N=1024 parameter cell. The paper also reports estimator-derived rows for larger signer counts; those larger rows are not separate implementation profiles in this artifact. Run: cd lemur-rs cargo run --release --bin lemur -- sizes cargo run --release --bin bench -- --fast cargo run --release --bin bench_verify -- --zero-fixture --n 1048576 --reps 1 Reproducing The Paper Implementation Table The paper's implementation-performance table reports the shipped tau=20, N=2^10 implementation cell plus extrapolated or estimator-derived entries for N in {2^15, 2^20}. Run the deterministic size calculations: cd lemur-rs cargo run --release --bin lemur -- sizes --n 1024 This reproduces the implemented aggregated-signature-size cell (N=2^10, 185.5 KB). The larger signature-size cells are predicted Rice-encoded sizes for the corresponding tau=20 rows in parameter/summary.txt, computed via: cd parameter python3 rice_sizes.py # totals only (paper Table 6 "Real" column) python3 rice_sizes.py --breakdown # tau=20 cells with KOTS vs HVC split python3 rice_sizes.py --all --breakdown # every (tau, N) cell, split Aggregate-size breakdown for the tau=20 cells (KB). KOTS and HVC totals sum (with a 1-byte attempt prefix) to the Rice-encoded total in the last column; the worst-case column is the Table 5 fixed-width upper bound from parameter/summary.txt. HVC dominates at every cell (~97% of the bytes), which is why the encoder only searches Rice for the HVC components — KOTS Z_agg is always fixed-width with an N-dependent bound. N Worst-case (Table 5) KOTS Z_agg HVC opening Rice-encoded total 2^10 232 KB 5.6 KB 179.9 KB 185.5 KB 2^15 315 KB 6.9 KB 257.6 KB 264.5 KB 2^20 444 KB 7.8 KB 371.7 KB 379.6 KB Rice compresses HVC only (the KOTS savings vs Table 5 — 7→5.6, 8→6.9, 9→7.8 KB — come from the N-dependent statistical bound on Z_agg, not Rice). At N=2^10 the HVC opening drops from 226 KB (Table 5) to 179.9 KB, a ~20% reduction; because HVC dominates the bytes (~97%) this carries through to the total, which drops from 232 KB to 185.5 KB. Run the main timing benchmark: cargo run --release --bin bench -- --fast This produces the measured N=2^10 entries used in the paper table: Row Source line Signing, BDS08 Stateful Signing (BDS08, mean ...) Aggregation, N=2^10 Secure Aggregation under --- Aggregation (N=1024) --- Batch verification, N=2^10 Batch Verify under --- Aggregation (N=1024) --- The tree-in-memory signing row is optional because it materializes the HVC tree and needs substantial RAM: cargo run --release --bin bench -- --fast --with-tree Use the Tree Sign (mean ...) line for the table. At tau=20, the tree allocation is about 8 GiB ((2^21 − 1) · ω · d · 8 B with ω=2, d=256). Run the large-N verification-only benchmark: cargo run --release --bin bench_verify -- --zero-fixture --n 32768 --reps 3 cargo run --release --bin bench_verify -- --zero-fixture --n 1048576 --reps 1 Use the Batch Verify mean lines for the N=2^15 and N=2^20 batch verification cells. The benchmark uses an accepting all-zero public-key and aggregate-signature fixture so it measures lemur_avrfy without first running large aggregation. The large-N aggregation cells in the paper table are marked as extrapolated. To recompute them, take the measured N=8192 Secure Aggregation time from bench --fast and scale linearly. This N=8192 benchmark is an extrapolation anchor and is not itself reported as a paper-table column: Aggregation(2^15) = Aggregation(8192) * 32768 / 8192 Aggregation(2^20) = Aggregation(8192) * 1048576 / 8192 For the 24-thread run on AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 used in the paper, Secure Aggregation at N=8192 measures 2.79 s (1 attempt on this fixture; the 2-unique-signer fixture replicated 4096-fold can occasionally force a retry, but a deployment with N distinct signers would not). Linear scaling gives approximately 11.2 s at N=2^15 and 6.0 min at N=2^20. To minimise jitter, use a stable thermal envelope (e.g. desktop / server) or pin the CPU frequency with cpupower frequency-set. Aggregation sub-step breakdown cargo run --release --bin bench_aggregate produces an end-to-end-to-sub-step attribution of lemur_aggregate and lemur_avrfy. Representative results at tau=20 on the same 24-thread machine: Aggregation (lemur_aggregate) sub-steps: Step N=1024 N=8192 Individual pre-verify (×N, rayon) 177.6 ms (15.4%) 1.31 s (46.7%) PK serialization (concat_pk_bytes) 6.2 ms (0.5%) 59.9 ms (2.1%) Randomizer derivation (SHAKE128) 5.4 ms (0.5%) 43.6 ms (1.6%) KOTS aggregate Σ wᵢ·zᵢ 9.8 ms (0.8%) 64.1 ms (2.3%) HVC opening aggregate Σ wᵢ·dᵢ 937.7 ms (81.2%) 1.32 s (47.2%) avrfy probe (close-loop check) 15.5 ms (1.3%) 113.7 ms (4.1%) End-to-end lemur_aggregate 1.16 s 2.80 s Batch verification (lemur_avrfy) sub-steps: Step N=1024 N=8192 PK serialization 6.2 ms (40.0%) 59.9 ms (52.6%) Randomizer derivation 5.3 ms (34.1%) 46.8 ms (41.1%) HVC commitment aggregate Σ wᵢ·Tᵢ 0.89 ms (5.8%) 5.63 ms (4.9%) HVC sVrfy (Babai decode + verify) 2.72 ms (17.5%) 1.30 ms (1.1%) KOTS sVrfy 0.56 ms (3.6%) 0.27 ms (0.2%) End-to-end lemur_avrfy 15.5 ms 114.0 ms bench_aggregate is also the source of the new NTT-domain aggregation microbenchmark used in the paper's implementation-notes section. Scope: this profile only measures the N=2^10 parameter cell The Rust artifact ships a single parameter profile, D256_K4, with profile.n_signers = 1024, beta_agg = 175 655, eta = 169, omega = 2, kappa = 5. The paper's N ∈ {2^15, 2^17, 2^20} rows are different parameter cells (larger k, m, omega, eta, beta_agg; see parameter/summary.txt), not just the same scheme at larger N. Running bench_aggregate at N > 8192 against the shipped profile would only stress-test it out of spec, not measure the paper's larger-N cells. For the paper's N=2^10 row, use the bench_aggregate numbers above. For N ∈ {2^15, 2^17, 2^20}: - Sizes: reproduce via python3 parameter/rice_sizes.py, which applies the Rice-encoding cost model to the appropriate summary.txt row (no separate implementation profile needed).

title: Dynamic Probability Distributions: A Bayesian Extension
abstract: This paper explores the application of Bayesian statistics to dynamic probability distributions, offering a novel approach to probabilistic reasoning and prediction. Traditional Bayesian methods often struggle with complex, evolving probability distributions. We extend the core concepts of Bayesian inference to dynamically update probability distributions based on observed data, enabling more accurate predictions and inference in scenarios where the underlying distribution changes over time. The core mechanism focuses on a dynamic update process that integrates the traditional Bayesian update with a system of continuous probability distributions. This integration allows for a more robust and adaptive approach to probabilistic modeling. The paper details the theoretical framework and practical implementation of this extension, demonstrating its effectiveness through illustrative examples, particularly in the context of time-series data analysis.

title: Probability Logic Algorithm Optimization for Adaptive Complexity
abstract: This paper presents a novel probabilistic logic algorithm designed for adaptive complexity optimization. Traditional probabilistic algorithms often employ a fixed complexity, failing to efficiently scale with input data size. This work introduces a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism to automatically tailor algorithm complexity, ensuring optimal performance across diverse data scenarios. The core of the innovation lies in a sophisticated algorithm that iteratively analyzes input data characteristics and adjusts the algorithm's complexity through a carefully constructed feedback loop. This adaptive approach directly addresses the limitations of static complexity models, leading to significant improvements in computational efficiency and scalability. The paper details the algorithm's design, its practical implementation, and empirical evaluation on benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling complex data.

title: 基于自适应的深度学习模型的正则化策略
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to deep learning model regularization, leveraging adaptive parameter and strength adjustments. Traditional regularization techniques often rely on fixed parameters, failing to adequately address the dynamic nature of complex datasets. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts regularization strength based on the input data's characteristics, significantly improving model generalization and stability. The core mechanism involves integrating a self-adaptive regularization scheme with a refined regularization strategy, enabling the model to automatically optimize its regularization parameters and strength in response to data variations. This approach offers a robust and flexible solution to the challenges of model calibration and robustness.

title: Quantum Topology-Based Self-Organized Computing Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-organizing computing framework leveraging quantum topology to dynamically adjust system topology and computational complexity. Traditional computing paradigms often rely on static configurations, limiting the potential for highly adaptive and efficient computation. We propose a framework that utilizes quantum topology principles to generate self-organizing systems capable of self-adjusting to complex problems, offering a fundamentally new approach to computational design. This framework aims to address limitations in traditional approaches by providing dynamic, adaptive, and potentially highly efficient solutions. The core mechanism focuses on manipulating the system's topology through quantum entanglement, allowing for effortless optimization of computational resources. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this approach and present preliminary results demonstrating the framework's effectiveness in solving a specific, albeit simplified, computational problem.

title: Title: Self-Organizing Quantum Networks for Data Distribution
abstract: Quantum networks, leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics, hold immense promise for secure communication and distributed quantum computation. Traditional quantum networks suffer from inherent limitations in scalability and data distribution. This paper presents a novel self-organizing quantum network architecture, designed to efficiently distribute quantum data across a network using dynamic state adjustment mechanisms. We propose a mechanism where nodes automatically configure their quantum states based on incoming data, fostering a self-configuring network topology. This contrasts sharply with static network designs, offering improved performance and adaptability. The core mechanism emphasizes the dynamic adjustment of quantum states, addressing a critical bottleneck in current quantum network research. This research explores the potential of this approach to enable efficient data routing and exploration of novel network topologies. The resulting network architecture demonstrates enhanced data distribution capabilities and opens avenues for practical applications in quantum information processing.

title: Contextualized Semantic Graph Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces Contextualized Semantic Graph Neural Networks (CSGNNs), a novel approach to graph representation learning that addresses the inherent limitations of static graph embeddings. Existing graph neural networks often struggle to adapt to evolving semantic relationships within graphs, primarily due to their inability to capture dynamic changes in node and edge meanings. CSGNNs propose a framework incorporating dynamic contextualization layers to learn and represent relationships based on the evolving semantic meaning. This is achieved through the integration of attention mechanisms trained on external knowledge graphs, providing a rich source of semantic information, and the incorporation of temporal modeling to capture changes in these relationships over time. The core claim is that augmenting standard Graph Neural Networks with these dynamic contextualization layers will significantly improve their performance in tasks requiring understanding of evolving graph structures. The resulting model demonstrates superior ability to learn and represent complex, dynamic relationships compared to static embedding methods. The key innovation lies in the ability to model semantic shifts, leading to more robust and accurate graph representations.

title: Information Entropy Dynamics Adaptive Matrix
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for machine learning model parameter optimization utilizing information entropy dynamics. The core principle is to dynamically adjust a matrix based on the calculated information entropy, fostering a self-adaptive learning process. Traditional parameter tuning methods often rely on fixed values, while this approach dynamically adjusts the matrix to improve model generalization and adaptability. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through experimental results, showcasing enhanced performance compared to existing techniques.

title: Explainable AI via Probabilistic Causal Graph Learning
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to developing explainable artificial intelligence (AI) by leveraging probabilistic causal graph learning. The core premise is that truly explainable AI requires the identification and representation of genuine causal relationships within data, translated into a readily interpretable probabilistic model. We introduce a mechanism that combines causal inference techniques with deep learning to automatically learn these causal structures. A critical element of this approach is the formalization of "causal uncertainty," providing a quantitative measure of confidence in the learned causal relationships. This framework offers a more robust and trustworthy method for generating explanations compared to traditional methods reliant on correlation alone. The proposed methodology addresses limitations in existing explainable AI techniques by grounding explanations in a verifiable causal structure. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework, outlining the key components and considerations for successful implementation.

title: Benchmarking 3D and 2.5D Convolutional and Transformer Architectures for Ovarian Tumour Classification on Clinical CT with Quantified Cross-Architecture Explanation Agreement
abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods are routinely reported alongside deep learning models for 2 medical imaging, yet whether architecturally distinct models attend to the same anatomy 3 when classifying the same scan is rarely examined. We address this question on a clinical 4 computed tomography cohort of 190 contrast-enhanced volumes from 165 patients acquired 5 through NHS Scotland, benchmarking fifteen architectures spanning three-dimensional 6 volumetric and 2.5D slice-based families under a common protocol with patient-level 7 stratified group cross-validation. Spatial overlap between Gradient-weighted Class Activa- 8 tion Mapping and Attention Rollout is then measured by an Intersection over Union on 9 percentile-thresholded maps, for which the chance level is analytically determined. Vision 10 Transformer Base/16 achieved the highest discrimination at an area under the curve of 11 0.896, while volumetric models ranked higher on accuracy than on discrimination. Substi- 12 tuting RadImageNet for ImageNet cost 4.7 and 24.2 percentage points of accuracy where 13 matched weights allowed a controlled comparison, a penalty comparable to the spread 14 across architectures. Mean explanation agreement was 0.336, three times the chance level 15 of 0.111, but 12.6% of volumes fell at or below chance and agreement proved decoupled 16 from predictive correctness. These results indicate that explanation agreement should not 17 be treated as a proxy for reliability without prior validation.

title: On the exact quantum chromatic number of generalized Johnson graphs
abstract: The quantum chromatic number is a fundamental parameter in the study of nonlocal games, capturing the extent to which entanglement can improve performance in distributed tasks. In this paper, we investigate the quantum chromatic number of generalized Johnson graphs. By constructing modulus-one orthogonal representations, we obtain general upper bounds on their quantum chromatic numbers. We further analyze the smallest eigenvalue of these graphs. Combining the resulting Hoffman-type lower bounds with the upper bounds obtained from orthogonal representations, we determine the exact quantum chromatic numbers of two infinite families of generalized Johnson graphs. Finally, applying a forbidden-distance theorem for binary codes, we show that the classical chromatic numbers of these families grow exponentially with $n$, whereas their quantum chromatic numbers grow linearly. These families exhibit an exponential separation between the classical and quantum chromatic numbers.

title: Quantum Topology Geometry Transformation Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm, the Quantum Topology Geometry Transformation Optimization Algorithm (QTGTA), designed to automatically adjust geometric transformations and precisely model complex geometric structures. The algorithm leverages quantum computation simulations to explore the intricate interplay of quantum topology and geometric transformations, providing a powerful tool for optimization and modeling. We present a framework where the algorithm iteratively refines geometric parameters through quantum simulations, resulting in enhanced accuracy and improved model representation. The core mechanism centers around utilizing quantum entanglement and superposition to explore a vast geometric space, enabling the discovery of optimal transformation strategies. This approach offers a fundamentally different pathway compared to traditional optimization methods, promising significant advancements in geometric modeling and data analysis.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Adaptive Parameter Adjustment Algorithm
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is a rapidly evolving field that leverages the unique properties of quantum systems to solve complex computational problems. Traditional machine learning algorithms often struggle with scaling to larger datasets and complex models, limiting their applicability in diverse domains. This paper introduces a novel adaptive parameter adjustment algorithm for quantum machine learning, aiming to address these limitations by dynamically adjusting model parameters during training. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously optimizes parameters based on observed performance, leading to improved model accuracy and generalization capabilities. The proposed algorithm offers a significant advancement over existing techniques by providing a more flexible and responsive approach to parameter tuning. This research explores the potential of this adaptive approach to enhance the performance of various quantum machine learning models.

abstract: This paper proposes a novel compression algorithm leveraging algorithmic self-similarity to achieve superior data compression. The proposed approach demonstrates significant improvements in compression ratios and efficiency, offering a fundamentally new method for data compression.

title: Hierarchical Verification of Concurrent Systems using Abstract Interpretation
abstract: Formal verification of concurrent systems is a critical technique for ensuring software reliability, particularly in safety-critical applications. However, traditional verification methods often suffer from prohibitive computational costs, especially as system complexity increases. This paper presents a novel hierarchical abstract interpretation framework designed to address this challenge. The core idea is to progressively refine the abstraction level of the concurrent system, starting with a coarse-grained abstraction and iteratively applying refinement steps to achieve a more precise representation while maintaining computational tractability. This hierarchical approach allows for scalable verification of complex system behavior, mitigating the exponential growth in verification time associated with traditional methods. The framework is built upon established abstract interpretation techniques, adapted and combined in a structured manner to exploit abstraction hierarchies. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and a detailed description of the framework's components and operation.

abstract: Human-validated Phase-2 expansion of the Fusha–Darija evaluation project. title: A Systematic Review of Hyper-Heuristics in Power System Optimization: Theory, Applications, and Future Directions
abstract: Modern power system optimization problems have become increasingly large-scale, non-convex, and highly constrained. Conventional optimization methods and metaheuristics struggle with these complexities, primarily due to premature convergence, extensive parameter-tuning requirements, and the limitations of the No Free Lunch theorem. To address these challenges, hyper-heuristics have emerged as high-level approaches that search the space of heuristics rather than the solution space directly, providing greater generality across different domains. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review searched Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Springer Nature Link, and Taylor & Francis Online for peer-reviewed studies published up to June 2026 on hyper-heuristics applied to power system optimization. Study eligibility was assessed based on topical relevance, and the findings were synthesized narratively. Out of 162 unique records screened, 21 studies were included in the final review without formal risk-of-bias restrictions. The findings indicate that while hyper-heuristics offer excellent efficiency, robustness, and solution quality, their overall application in power systems remains limited. Current research relies heavily on selection-based architectures, leaving significant gaps in computational time reporting and real-world grid testing. Future research should extend selection-based methods, explore wider problem variants, address underexplored power system optimization domains, and investigate the development of generation hyper-heuristics.

evidence.title: A Systematic Review of Hyper-Heuristics in Power System Optimization: Theory, Applications, and Future Directions
evidence.abstract: Modern power system optimization problems have become increasingly large-scale, non-convex, and highly constrained. Conventional optimization methods and metaheuristics struggle with these complexities, primarily due to premature convergence, extensive parameter-tuning requirements, and the limitations of the No Free Lunch theorem. To address these challenges, hyper-heuristics have emerged as high-level approaches that search the space of heuristics rather than the solution space directly, providing greater generality across different domains. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review searched Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Springer Nature Link, and Taylor & Francis Online for peer-reviewed studies published up to June 2026 on hyper-heuristics applied to power system optimization. Study eligibility was assessed based on topical relevance, and the findings were synthesized narratively. Out of 162 unique records screened, 21 studies were included in the final review without formal risk-of-bias restrictions. The findings indicate that while hyper-heuristics offer excellent efficiency, robustness, and solution quality, their overall application in power systems remains limited. Current research relies heavily on selection-based architectures, leaving significant gaps in computational time reporting and real-world grid testing. Future research should extend selection-based methods, explore wider problem variants, address underexplored power system optimization domains, and investigate the development of generation hyper-heuristics.

title: Experience over Hierarchy: Industry Tenure, Technology Exposure, and Fourth Industrial Revolution Awareness Among Hotel Managers in Gauteng, South Africa
abstract: Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) technologies are resetting hotel operations, guest experiences, and workforce dynamics. This study investigates awareness of 4IR technologies among managerial employees in three- to five-star hotels in Gauteng, South Africa, with particular attention to industry experience, formal job level, hotel star grading, perceived benefits, and direct organisational exposure to implemented technologies. A quantitative, descriptive, cross-sectional survey used a structured questionnaire completed by 146 managerial employees. Descriptive statistics, cross-tabulations, chi-square tests, and Fisher’s exact tests were used. Years of industry experience were significantly associated with awareness (chi-square(3) = 13.56, p = 0.004), with the 11–15-year group reporting the highest proportion of greater awareness (78.38%). Job level (p = 0.236) and hotel star grading (p = 0.155) were not significantly associated with awareness. Artificial intelligence implementation (p = 0.043), Internet of Things implementation (p = 0.006), and perceived operational benefits (p = 0.001) were significantly associated with awareness. Interpreted through an integrated technology-adoption framework, the findings indicate that mid-career experience and direct technology exposure are more closely associated with awareness than formal hierarchy or luxury classification.

title: Architectures Defining Graph Neural Networks
abstract: A fundamental construction for complex interrelationships in domains such as natural science, finance, social networking, and recommendation systems is a simple data structure called graph which is real world systems are expressed through. The management of non-Euclidean data structures, which are graph-based, pose exceptional challenges because of their irregularity compared to traditional machine learning approaches which rely on grid structured data. By means of deep learning techniques, GNNs are able to manage optimally graph-structured data efficiently. There has been a marked advancement in GNN design in recent years with regards to scaling issues and over-smoothing in addition to enhancing their capability to learn efficient representations. Learning on graphs was made possible by early GNN models like Spectral Based Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and spatial based Graph SAGE and Graph Attention Networks (GATs). In the detection of fraudulent data and peer referral, Graph Neural Networks improve the effectiveness of social network analysis. During drug development, they help forecast molecular traits and probe protein interactions for the analysis. In the creation of tailored recommendations, GNNs are employed in recommendation systems, while in cyber defense, they scrutinize networks for intrusion anomalies and fraudulent activities. Furthermore, GNNs offer more complex graph-based learning, affecting disciplines such as natural language processing, traffic prediction, and financial modeling. Considering their achievements, GNNs are still facing a number of obstacles, such as the need for improved interpretability, computational inefficiencies, and trouble managing dynamic graphs. Resolving these problems is essential to increasing their usefulness and enhancing their functionality in a variety of applications. The development of GNN designs, their main practical uses, and the persisting difficulties are all thoroughly covered in this study. This paper explores the evolution of GNN architectures, highlighting key innovations, their limitations, applications and future research directions.

title: Graph‐Based Anomaly Detection in Cybersecurity and FinTech
abstract: The complexity of cyberattacks and financial fraud has seen the need for sophisticated anomaly detection techniques that extend beyond rule-based or statistical methods. Graph-Based Anomaly Detection (GAD) is a revolutionary approach, employing graphs to represent complex relationships within security and financial networks. This chapter delves into the usage of GAD in FinTech and cybersecurity through a focus on implementation-focused methods employing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in fraud detection as well as network security. Experiments show that GraphSAGE is effective in managing dynamic security and fraud networks, GCN is stable in structured graph settings, and GCT-GNN has better accuracy using transformer-based attention mechanisms. These results emphasize the promise of GNN-based methods for identifying anomalies not only in cybersecurity but also in anti-money laundering, synthetic identity fraud, and insider trading anomalies. One of the main contributions of the chapter is the application and testing of three state-of-the-art GNN models, GraphSAGE, Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), and Graph Convolutional Transformer-GNN (GCT-GNN), on network intrusion detection based on the UNSW-NB15 dataset. The study illustrates that GraphSAGE performs better in dynamic networks, GCN is more stable under structured graph settings, and GCT-GNN enhances detection accuracy with attention mechanisms. Experimental evaluations demonstrate robust performance in metrics such as AUC-ROC, precision, recall, and F1-score. In addition to that, this chapter discusses the challenges in scalability, adversarial attacks, explainability, and real-time fraud detection. Some of the future directions of research involve self-supervised learning, graph contrastive learning, and hybrid GNN models.

title: Concord: A Video Relational Algebra for Cross-Modal Query Optimization
abstract: Semantic video queries let users embed natural language prompts and use multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to interpret the video. Such queries are increasingly popular for querying video data. However, their expressiveness comes at a steep cost: an MLLM may process hours of media to return only seconds of relevant output, making naive execution slow, expensive, and inaccurate. We propose Concord, a system for expressing and optimizing semantic video queries. We makes three contributions. First, we introduce Video Relational Algebra (VRA), a nested algebra over videos, transcripts, frames, and object tracks that captures common semantic video operations. Second, we derive a set of approximate optimizations that rewrite VRA queries to reduce MLLM usage while improving result quality. For narrated video, Concord either processes transcripts instead of video or uses them to identify video clips for MLLM processing. For cross-camera queries without narration, detection and tracking replace a whole-video MLLM join with a track-level relational join. Third, we evaluate Concord on real-world videos. Across 4.59 hours of soccer broadcasts and 3.92 hours of lectures, transcript-to-video queries send only 5.32% and 2.47% of source-video duration to the MLLM and reduce MLLM cost by up to 87%. In two five-second highway clips with 18 manually adjudicated cross-camera vehicles, a Detect-Track-Join query improves F1 from .364 to .813 while making no MLLM calls. See our project at https://concord-db.github.io/.

title: Self-Supervised Lexical Representation Learning for Fast, Large-Scale Phylogenetic Inference
abstract: Computational phylogenetics has become an essential tool in historical linguistics, yet its application at a global scale remains constrained by two factors: the labor-intensive manual annotation of cognacy judgments required for character-based methods and the substantial computational cost of inference on large datasets. This paper introduces a fully self-supervised contrastive learning framework that learns lexical representations directly from raw IPA-transcribed wordlists, without requiring cognacy annotations, alignments, or additional expert input. The model employs a dual contrastive objective: a word-level loss that organizes phonetically similar forms into a coherent space, and an auxiliary language-level loss that encourages the lexical space to reflect broader phonological properties of languages. From the resulting word representations, pairwise language distances are derived and used to infer a global phylogenetic tree of 3,399 language varieties. The inferred tree achieves a generalized quartet distance (GQD) to the Glottolog reference tree competitive with multiple baselines, while requiring only minutes of computation on a standard notebook GPU. Furthermore, the same representations capture diachronic concept stability: variance in pairwise distances across languages yields stability rankings that correlate significantly with established rankings. Ablation studies confirm that both the language-level objective and the use of phonetic feature vectors improved the inferred trees topology with regards to GQD. The framework thus provides a computationally efficient and fully automatic alternative for large-scale phylogenetic inference and offers a unified representation supporting downstream analyses at both the language and concept level.

title: Designing for the Else: Generating AI Specifications That Handle What Is Not There
abstract: I can generate a working AI specification in about five minutes, and it runs across five different AI platforms without being rewritten for each one. This paper describes the method that got me there and how I checked that it was real. The method is a loop. Build a specification for a job, test it, then pull out the parts that were not about that job, strip the job-specific language, and put them where the next build will load them. Over fourteen builds the extraction got smaller each pass until the specification-writing work was nearly gone. What survived extraction was almost entirely else clauses: what to do when an answer is absent, unverifiable, or open to more than one reading. Handed an unspecified case, a model does not stop. It fills the gap fluently, and the filled version is indistinguishable from the real one. The failure is missing instructions rather than wrong ones. The method's weakest step is the extraction, and skipping it feels exactly like the loop converging. Version discipline kept separate from the loop is what let me find out that I had stopped. I checked my own reading of the corpus by giving the build records to a separate model session with the hypothesis withheld. The limits are stated plainly: one author, one domain, and no measured results.

title: A Generative Framework for Correlated Failure in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Asymptotic Floors, Dilution Thresholds, and Defense Stack Certification
abstract: Ensemble aggregation, defense-in-depth guardrails, and multi-agent workflows fundamentally pre-suppose component failure independence. In this work, we prove that shared pretraining blindspots and latent difficulty correlation induce severe Common Mode Failures (CMF) that render multiplicative reliability bounds invalid. First, we prove the K-Layer Defense Composition Theorem, deriving the asymptotic attack floor ϖharm > 0 and verification discount DK (ρ), explaining why stacked defenses fail to compound exponentially and validating our predictions against the empirical measurements of Alotaibi et al. (2026). Second, we establish the Sub-Majority Capability Dilution Theorem (K†) and the fundamental CMF Duality: while latent difficulty correlation cushions sub-majority committees (α < 1−ϖ2 ) against deterministic collapse (F∞ < 100%), finite consensus systematically dilutes accuracy relative to standalone champions, explaining why pooled SWE-bench Verified consensus degrades resolution from 40.6% (Top-1) to 32.6% (Top-9, p = 7.2 × 10−7; 31.10% under randomized tie-break at K = 10). Third, we establish the ϖ/ρ Identification Theorem: pairwise correlation (K = 2) is fundamentally unidentifiable, whereas K ≥ 3 agent pools achieve local identifiability on the interior parameter space via joint co-failure moments. Across 11, 710 benchmark evaluations (11, 442 unique tasks across 38 models), within-suite splits confirm that error correlation tracks task structure at fixed model pool: multi-step competition mathematics induces heavy correlation ( ¯ϕ = 0.6667) versus general reasoning ( ¯ϕ = 0.5140) across the identical seven 2026 frontier reasoning models. Finally, we derive the Assume-Guarantee Safety Composition Operator, providing model-based safety formulas that capture joint tail correlation.

title: Dynamic Probability Field Theory Model Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of dynamic probability field theory models through the utilization of a novel, adaptive optimization algorithm. Traditional probabilistic models often rely on static parameter and structural configurations, failing to effectively adapt to evolving data or changing environmental conditions. This research proposes a framework that dynamically adjusts model parameters and structure, leading to enhanced predictive accuracy in complex systems. The core mechanism centers on leveraging the inherent dynamic nature of probability field theory models to automate parameter and structural refinement, addressing the limitations of static optimization methods. We present a robust optimization strategy that incorporates feedback loops, ensuring continuous refinement and improved model performance. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, provides experimental validation demonstrating its efficacy, and discusses potential future research directions.

title: ##拓扑量子计算的自适应几何结构
abstract: Quantum computing, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics, holds immense potential across diverse fields, from drug discovery to materials science. However, the design and optimization of quantum algorithms often rely on meticulously crafted quantum states. This paper explores the innovative application of 拓扑量子计算 (Topological Quantum Computing), specifically focusing on the dynamic adjustment of quantum bit (qubit) states to enhance algorithmic efficiency. We propose a novel approach utilizing a dynamically generated "拓扑张量" (Topological Tensor) – a mathematical construct designed to reflect the inherent quantum properties – to guide the evolution of qubit configurations. This method aims to surpass existing algorithms through enhanced optimization and improved accuracy in quantum computation. The core mechanism involves calculating the co-conjugate matrix of the topological tensor, allowing for real-time adaptation of qubit states. This research presents a framework for leveraging this dynamic geometry to unlock new possibilities in quantum algorithm design and performance. The paper will detail the theoretical underpinnings of this approach, present preliminary experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of the dynamic geometry, and discuss future research directions.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Monte Carlo Simulation of Complex Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to accelerate Monte Carlo simulations of complex networks by integrating quantum superposition into the core algorithm. We demonstrate a practical implementation of a quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo simulation, achieving significant speedups compared to classical methods for certain network configurations. The core mechanism involves utilizing quantum superposition to explore multiple states simultaneously, reducing the computational complexity inherent in traditional Monte Carlo techniques. The research explores the potential of this approach to unlock insights into intricate network dynamics, offering a pathway for enhanced analysis of complex systems. We provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance and discuss future directions for further investigation.

title: Dynamic Geometry Constraints and Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic geometry constraints and adaptive machine learning to complex data analysis. Traditional machine learning often relies on manually tuned parameters, limiting the model's flexibility and potential for robust feature learning. We propose a novel framework that dynamically adjusts the geometry of the data structure, enabling the model to automatically learn and recognize complex data characteristics. The core mechanism involves a synergistic interaction between geometric constraints and probabilistic distributions, allowing for a more efficient and adaptable representation of data. This approach offers a significant advancement in the ability of machine learning models to handle intricate data patterns and achieve superior performance across a variety of applications.

title: 基于图的神经网络的自适应架构优化
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to neural network architecture optimization utilizing graph-based representations. Traditional network architectures often lack adaptability, requiring manual tuning for specific datasets. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts the structure of a neural network by representing it as a graph, leveraging self-adaptive algorithms to enhance model performance. The core mechanism involves constructing a graph representing the network's connections and then employing an optimization algorithm to refine this graph, effectively creating a more robust and adaptable model. The advantages of this approach include improved generalization, faster training times, and the capacity to handle complex data distributions. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this method.

title: Quantum Entanglement Dynamic Topology Optimization (QDOT) Framework
abstract: Quantum entanglement offers a unique and potentially transformative approach to optimization, particularly in the realm of quantum systems. This paper explores the application of a novel dynamic topology optimization framework, the QDOT framework, leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement to achieve unprecedented performance improvements in quantum computation. We detail the core mechanism of this framework, focusing on the dynamic nature of entanglement-induced topology changes, and demonstrate its potential to overcome limitations of existing optimization techniques. The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the framework's design, implementation, and preliminary results, highlighting its advantages and future research directions.

title: Non-Euclidean Quantum State Collapse for Simulation
abstract: This paper explores a novel quantum state collapse algorithm predicated on the principles of non-Euclidean space. Traditional collapse mechanisms, while effective, often restrict the search space for potential solutions, limiting the exploration of quantum states. We propose a fundamentally different approach – utilizing a non-Euclidean representation of the quantum state – to significantly expand the range of possible solutions and increase the computational efficiency of state collapse. This investigation centers around a mechanism that allows the algorithm to navigate and manipulate states within a potentially higher-dimensional space, offering a pathway to explore a broader range of quantum configurations than conventional methods. The core claim is that this novel algorithm, leveraging non-Euclidean space, will dramatically enhance the capability of quantum state collapse.

title: Quantum Information-Driven Neural Network Structure Design
abstract: Quantum Information-Driven Neural Network Structure Design explores a novel approach to neural network architecture design leveraging quantum information to dynamically adjust network structure. This research introduces a method that automatically optimizes network topology, enhancing model performance and stability through a quantum-enhanced adaptation process. The core mechanism centers on utilizing quantum entanglement and superposition to represent and manipulate network parameters, leading to a more robust and adaptable system. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical framework and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in enhancing neural network capabilities.

abstract: Quantum topology, a fascinating field of physics, offers a novel approach to quantum algorithm optimization. The core mechanism leverages the unique properties of quantum topology to optimize quantum circuits, promising significant breakthroughs in the field of quantum computation. The proposed system offers a departure from traditional static optimization techniques, opening up new avenues for quantum algorithm development and performance enhancement.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Constraints for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper explores the application of non-Euclidean constraint methods to machine learning, aiming to enhance robustness and generalization. Traditional machine learning algorithms often struggle with sensitivity to initial conditions and feature space variations, leading to suboptimal performance. We introduce a novel constraint framework that allows for the definition of a non-Euclidean space, enabling the model to explore a wider range of possible solutions during training. This approach mitigates the limitations of conventional methods by introducing a dynamic, non-linear interaction between the model and the learning process. The core mechanism focuses on iteratively refining the model's representation through a process of constraint application and refinement, resulting in improved generalization capabilities. We present a theoretical framework for assessing the effectiveness of this approach and demonstrate its practical application through illustrative examples. The core claim is that incorporating this constraint method will significantly improve the performance of machine learning models across a range of tasks, particularly those involving complex data or high-dimensional spaces.

title: Decoder-Relative Predictive Learnability: A Sharp Approximation-to-Correlation Transfer Bound
abstract: Two representations can carry the same recoverable information about a target -- the best correlation any predictor achieves -- while differing in what a fixed, restricted decoder class can access. We formalize this gap through the representation-induced Bayes function g_R(r) = E[Y | R=r] and its normalized best-approximation error E_{F_P}(g_R) within a decoder class F_P. For any class closed under negation, the population gap satisfies G_D^pop <= A*_rho Phi(E_{F_P}(g_R)) with Phi(e) = 1 - sqrt(1-e); the bound holds with equality whenever F_P is scale-closed, a condition met by ridge and kernel-ridge subspaces and by fixed-width neural networks. The proofs are elementary, and we state which ingredients are classical. We give a finite-sample estimator of E_{F_P}(g_R), consistent for a fixed-partition variant, and evaluate the predictions on two simulated systems. On Lorenz-63 the bound holds in 68 of 84 replicate-mean checks for informative representations, with the violations concentrated in two representations. On a 1D Ising chain the experiment checks only the stability of the estimator under Nystrom approximation, on a representation with little predictive content. Version v4 (package version 2.0) replaces the manuscript and supplementary material of the earlier versions by the version revised after an audit against a journal's reviewing criteria; the validation code is unchanged. The changes are listed in the README of the package (Version history).

title: Development of an annotated dataset of persuasion strategies and initial testing of a natural language processing tool to detect persuasion strategies in text
abstract: In this project, we have worked on the development of a natural-language processing tool to support the automation of persuasive dialogue detection within large corpora of text. The corpus has been generated using a framework for persuasion strategies (Muir et al., 2022) which consists of conversational moves which a persuader will use to achieve their overarching persuasive aim. Seven dominant strategies are identified in this framework: Rapport and liking, Negotiating, Appeals to emotion, Appeals to logic, Appeals to authority, Social proof and Overt persuasion, manipulation, and pressure. This framework was used to annotate the Persuasion for Good corpus (Wang et al. 2019) and we then conducted a series of studies to test whether our model can accurately identify conversations in which attempted persuasion is known to be present, and created a classifier for predicting the probabilities of a given persuasion move being present in any given utterance. We present the initial results of these studies and discuss the implications of using the classifier to identify where both benign and malicious forms of persuasion are taking place in online conversations.

title: Emotion as a Distribution: Joint Valence-Arousal Probability Learning for Speaker-Independent Multimodal Emotion Recognition
abstract: Human emotion is graded and frequently mixed, yet most multimodal recognizers collapse it onto a single hard label. We argue the recognizer should instead expose a distribution over affective space. Our text+speech system, alongside its categorical decision, emits a $9\times9$ probability matrix over the Valence-Arousal plane, trained with a two-dimensional Gaussian soft target under a Kullback-Leibler/cross-entropy objective, aimed at counseling support. Evaluation is strict: speaker-independent 5-fold leave-one-session-out IEMOCAP with rotating-session inner validation, headline metrics only on the held-out session. Within one fixed encoder-fusion-head pipeline we compare Transformer and state-space (Mamba-1/2/3) backbones at matched depth and width, at two operating points ($T\approx550$, $T\approx2750$). The featured dual-head system reaches 73.0% $\pm$ 0.3 unweighted accuracy over three seeds (separate rerun: 72.1%), exceeding the Transformer fusion baseline by 3.0 UA points (95% session-bootstrap CI [1.0,4.7]; significant under paired t-test and session-level bootstrap), with no latency or memory advantage at these lengths; swapping the ~1M trainable front-end for frozen WavLM-Large features (learnable layer weights) lifts the same architecture to 76.6% $\pm$ 1.3. Pre-specified controls scope the claims honestly: simpler valence-arousal auxiliaries reproduce the classification lift within noise, and a dedicated regression head tracks the continuous ratings slightly better, so the head's specific value is the normalized affect distribution itself. That distribution recovers the circumplex: its center of mass tracks valence and arousal (CCC 0.66/0.66; predominantly between-class structure, weaker within-class tracking), and its entropy is weakly but consistently linked to categorical rater ambiguity, not dimensional spread.

title: Temporal Residual Neural Radiance Fields for Monocular Video Dynamic Human Body Reconstruction
abstract: In the field of computer vision and graphics, high-quality reconstruction of the human body in static scenes has been achieved in recent years by a single multilayer perceptron (MLP) in a number of approaches. However, MLPs have capacity limitations, requiring substantial training time and computational resources for dynamic scene reconstruction. And the quality of reconstruction is significantly constrained. This paper proposes a method for effectively processing complex spatiotemporal signals in dynamic scene human 3D modeling. The proposed method uses Temporal Residual Neural Radiance Fields to achieve novel view rendering and new pose synthesis of human bodies.To address the problem of representing temporal signals in video sequences, we construct a temporal residual field which is not related to the MLP architecture. Secondly, to improve reconstruction efficiency, we propose an integrated approach that reduces trainable parameters and accelerates rendering, thereby enhancing the network's feature representation capability. Finally, we design a multi-dimensional loss function to accurately measure the loss between predicted and actual spatial pixel values. The experimental results show that our proposed approach improves the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM) accuracy metrics compared to the latest representative methods. It maintains similar accuracy to Anim-NeRF and Neural Body while achieving a nearly 780-fold increase in time efficiency.

title: A Fairness Audit of the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern Method: Format-Specific and Gender-Differential Bias, with an Interpretable Calibration Layer for Cricket Target Revision
abstract: The Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (DLS) method has been the international standard for revising target scores in rain-interrupted limited-overs cricket since 1999. Despite over two decades of operational use, no large-scale empirical audit of its prediction bias has been published. We conduct such an audit on 8,150 international matches (3,095 ODIs, 5,055 T20Is) from Cricsheet, generating 233,550 synthetic interruption scenarios with temporal splits. We document two structured biases. First, DLS prediction error spans a 137-run range across (overs-remaining, wickets-lost) match-state buckets. Second, DLS exhibits a gender-differential bias on ODIs that has not previously been quantified: on the training split, mean over-prediction is +1.51 runs for men but +7.63 runs for women, a gap of +6.13 runs (F = 195.16, p < 10^-43). We benchmark DLS against five modern alternatives: Bi-LSTM, XGBoost, an enriched XGBoost variant, a deep context-aware model, and a stacking ensemble, and propose DLS-Cal, a lightweight interpretable calibration layer (27K parameters) outputting a state-conditioned correction added to DLS. DLS-Cal reduces absolute bias by 31% on ODI and 19% on T20I, and a gender-aware variant reduces women's ODI residual bias from +6.19 to +0.65 runs while leaving men's calibration unchanged. We release code, models, and data.

title: NLTS Hamiltonians from Good Quantum Codes
abstract: Abstract. The no low-energy trivial state (NLTS) conjecture of Freedman and Hastings [ Quantum Inf. Comput., 14 (2014), pp. 144–180] posits that there exist families of Hamiltonians with all low energy states of nontrivial complexity (with complexity measured by the quantum circuit depth preparing the state). We prove this conjecture by showing that families of constant-rate and linear-distance qLDPC codes correspond to NLTS local Hamiltonians.

title: A Study on Impact of Generative AI on Investment Decision-making at Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd.
abstract: This study, titled "A Study On Impact Of Generative AI On Investment Decisionmaking At Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd.," evaluates the operational effectiveness and financial feasibility of deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI (GenAI) in wealth management and equity research. In modern financial markets, the sheer volume of unstructured data—including corporate earnings transcripts, regulatory filings, financial news, and global market announcements—creates a cognitive bottleneck for research analysts. Traditional numerical predictive algorithms are incapable of synthesizing qualitative text files. This research explores how customized enterprise GenAI architectures automate research report writing, client query resolution, and sentiment summarization. A 5-year capital budgeting analysis (2021-2025) of a bank-led sensor deployment program is conducted using capital budgeting metrics, including Net Present Value (NPV), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), Payback Period (PBP), and Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR). The data indicates that the deployment of GenAI solutions improved analyst productivity by saving an average of 12.5 hours per week on report writing, while GenAI-optimized portfolios consistently generated excess returns (alpha) over the Nifty 50 Index. The financial evaluation yields a positive NPV of 392.4 Crores and an IRR of 45.1%, far exceeding the cost of capital. The study concludes that integrating Generative AI into investment workflows is highly financially feasible and operationally sustainable, providing a significant competitive advantage for modern asset management institutions. Keywords: Generative AI, Large Language Models (LLMs), Investment Decision-Making, Motilal Oswal, Analyst Productivity, Portfolio Performance, Cost-Benefit Analysis.

title: Native Cognition Kernel (NCK) 0.1
abstract: Native Cognition Kernel (NCK) 0.1 — Rust Technical Implementation and Proof of ConceptThis release contains the complete NCK 0.1 technical implementation package, including the Rust runtime, executable proof of concept, tests, mathematical reference materials, provenance records, reproducibility documentation, technical handoff materials, and release-integrity manifests.The package is designed to be built, tested, and executed locally, allowing independent developers and researchers to reproduce and inspect the demonstrated NCK behavior directly from the released source.The included NCK_MATHEMATICS_0.1.md remains the sole normative mathematical authority. title: Humanᴬᴵ and Orgᴬᴵ Framework Calculator
abstract: Humanᴬᴵ and Orgᴬᴵ Framework Calculator is a local-first interpretive software companion to the whitepaper Humanᴬᴵ and Orgᴬᴵ: A Relational Framework for AI-Mediated Human and Organizational Capacity. Version 1.2.0 produces a reproducible and defensible assessment record for a bounded domain, an assessment that another party can reload, verify and contest. An exported record satisfies the whitepaper's minimum reporting convention on its own: unit analysed, task, context, AI configuration, observation period, validation method, and boundary of accountability. The calculator provides a structured implementation of six components of the framework: 1. Epistemic decoupling assessment;2. Propagation exposure analysis;3. Constitutive Orgᴬᴵ threshold assessment;4. Material AI contribution analysis;5. Humanᴬᴵ and Orgᴬᴵ relational synergy;6. Maturity classification. It additionally implements two constructs defined elsewhere in the same whitepaper, the classification worksheet and membership test, and the Orgᴬᴵ evaluation profile, together with anti-pattern detection read against the entered configuration. Section 11.5 of whitepaper v1.5 describes the 1.0.0 companion and predates this release; nothing is redefined here, and the accompanying README carries the reconciliation. Principal changes in 1.2.0. Material contribution is evaluated across all seven dimensions of the individual outcome profile rather than a single selected dimension, and is demonstrated when the declared threshold is exceeded on at least one relevant dimension; results are not compressed into a composite score.Epistemic decoupling is entered as counts over a declared task set and reported with a 95% confidence interval, so that a gap measured on few tasks is not presented as a demonstrated finding. Each organizational criterion carries an evidence reference and evidence type; a criterion declared demonstrated without a reference is reported as declared but undocumented and does not contribute to the threshold. Validated organizational learning is shown as the seventh, non-constitutive component of the organizational architecture, conditioning only the cumulative maturity state. Propagation exposure is computed for the current configuration and for the state after declared controls. Maturity is assigned per bounded domain, with domains in which AI is prohibited recorded as such rather than levelled. The assessment record uses JSON schema version 2 and can be reimported, including migration of records produced by versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0. The interface prints the assessment as a standalone document. No formula defined in the whitepaper was altered, and the six assertions of the original test suite pass unmodified. The software is designed to support structured interpretation of user-entered evidence. It does not independently verify the accuracy, completeness, provenance, or sufficiency of that evidence. Calculations are performed locally in the user's browser. The application does not require user accounts, does not contain an application database, and does not transmit assessment data to a remote analysis service. This release makes no network request of any kind: typefaces are embedded in the file, so the calculator operates unchanged on an isolated network. Nothing is persisted in the browser. The self-hosted build carries a Content Security Policy with connect-src 'none', which allows these properties to be verified rather than assumed. Tests ship with the release and extract the implemented logic from the delivered file, so a passing run is a statement about the artefact itself. The calculator does not provide empirical validation, certification, legal advice, compliance determination, or an automated organizational decision. evidence.title: Humanᴬᴵ and Orgᴬᴵ Framework Calculator
evidence.abstract: Humanᴬᴵ and Orgᴬᴵ Framework Calculator is a local-first interpretive software companion to the whitepaper Humanᴬᴵ and Orgᴬᴵ: A Relational Framework for AI-Mediated Human and Organizational Capacity. Version 1.2.0 produces a reproducible and defensible assessment record for a bounded domain, an assessment that another party can reload, verify and contest. An exported record satisfies the whitepaper's minimum reporting convention on its own: unit analysed, task, context, AI configuration, observation period, validation method, and boundary of accountability. The calculator provides a structured implementation of six components of the framework: 1. Epistemic decoupling assessment;2. Propagation exposure analysis;3. Constitutive Orgᴬᴵ threshold assessment;4. Material AI contribution analysis;5. Humanᴬᴵ and Orgᴬᴵ relational synergy;6. Maturity classification. It additionally implements two constructs defined elsewhere in the same whitepaper, the classification worksheet and membership test, and the Orgᴬᴵ evaluation profile, together with anti-pattern detection read against the entered configuration. Section 11.5 of whitepaper v1.5 describes the 1.0.0 companion and predates this release; nothing is redefined here, and the accompanying README carries the reconciliation. Principal changes in 1.2.0. Material contribution is evaluated across all seven dimensions of the individual outcome profile rather than a single selected dimension, and is demonstrated when the declared threshold is exceeded on at least one relevant dimension; results are not compressed into a composite score.Epistemic decoupling is entered as counts over a declared task set and reported with a 95% confidence interval, so that a gap measured on few tasks is not presented as a demonstrated finding. Each organizational criterion carries an evidence reference and evidence type; a criterion declared demonstrated without a reference is reported as declared but undocumented and does not contribute to the threshold. Validated organizational learning is shown as the seventh, non-constitutive component of the organizational architecture, conditioning only the cumulative maturity state. Propagation exposure is computed for the current configuration and for the state after declared controls. Maturity is assigned per bounded domain, with domains in which AI is prohibited recorded as such rather than levelled. The assessment record uses JSON schema version 2 and can be reimported, including migration of records produced by versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0. The interface prints the assessment as a standalone document. No formula defined in the whitepaper was altered, and the six assertions of the original test suite pass unmodified. The software is designed to support structured interpretation of user-entered evidence. It does not independently verify the accuracy, completeness, provenance, or sufficiency of that evidence. Calculations are performed locally in the user's browser. The application does not require user accounts, does not contain an application database, and does not transmit assessment data to a remote analysis service. This release makes no network request of any kind: typefaces are embedded in the file, so the calculator operates unchanged on an isolated network. Nothing is persisted in the browser. The self-hosted build carries a Content Security Policy with connect-src 'none', which allows these properties to be verified rather than assumed. Tests ship with the release and extract the implemented logic from the delivered file, so a passing run is a statement about the artefact itself. The calculator does not provide empirical validation, certification, legal advice, compliance determination, or an automated organizational decision. Its outputs must be interpreted in relation to the definitions, assumptions, boundaries, and limitations established in the accompanying whitepaper. title: Algorithmic Self-Organization of Abstract Data Structures
abstract: This paper explores the potential of algorithmic self-organization to generate complex, self-organizing data structures. Traditional algorithm design often relies on predefined rules and iterations, whereas this work proposes a method that leverages abstract specifications to drive the creation of novel structures. The core mechanism involves a generative process that produces abstract representations, which then evolve into a complex structure, fostering emergent behavior and allowing for the creation of algorithms with unique properties. The paper details the methodology, provides illustrative examples, and discusses the implications of this approach for the design of advanced data structures and algorithms.

title: 基于自适应量子网络的自适应数据处理
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to data processing utilizing a dynamically adaptive quantum network. Traditional quantum computing paradigms often struggle with the complexities of large datasets, necessitating inefficient processing methods. This work proposes a system where quantum network parameters are dynamically adjusted to optimize data analysis and processing, resulting in significantly enhanced efficiency and accuracy compared to classical approaches. The core mechanism relies on exploiting the unique properties of quantum entanglement and superposition to accelerate computations and minimize errors. We detail the system architecture, the algorithm for parameter adaptation, and the resulting performance improvements across a range of data processing tasks. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential impact of this technology on various fields requiring large-scale data analysis.

title: Dynamic Quantum Topology Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum topology modeling approach employing machine learning to automatically learn and model complex quantum topologies, and to enable dynamic optimization. Traditional topology modeling relies on manual parameter definition, which is computationally intensive. Our method leverages machine learning to autonomously model topology and then utilizes machine learning to dynamically optimize the topology, improving efficiency. The core mechanism involves learning a representation of the topology through machine learning, followed by applying optimization techniques to refine the topology. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in modeling specific quantum topological structures and provide a framework for applying it to other topology problems. The resulting models offer a significant advancement over existing approaches, particularly in terms of automation and efficiency.

title: Symmetry Groups of the Platonic Solid POVMs: Binary Polyhedral Groups as Quantum Circuits
abstract: We study the symmetry groups of the Platonic solid POVMs: the binary polyhedral groups 2T, 2O, and 2I, exact unitary 2-, 3-, and 5-designs. A unified treatment, bringing together mathematical construction, quantum circuits, and cost, is missing. We provide it, in the single-qubit setting, via two complementary constructions and a compilation, implemented with symbolic computation. The result is an atlas of all 192 group elements, fully reproducible from accompanying code, its gate sequences, none deeper than four, doubling as POVM rotation circuits. Once anchored to the Pauli group, 2T and 2O are entirely Clifford, while the binary icosahedral group 2I requires at most one non-Clifford gate per element—the golden gate Φ. As a double-coset decomposition, 2I = 2T ⊔ 2T Φ 2T. We prove that only the octahedral POVM admits exact implementation over our gate sets (Clifford+T among them), and never deterministically; in our orientation, the other four point at magic states. We consider the POVMs in classical shadow estimation, where an inexact implementation is paid for in estimator variance; scalability keeps us to local shadows, a per-qubit factorized regime. We compare two randomized implementations: both support robust shadow estimation, but calibrate different scalars; calibration must match protocol. Every Platonic solid POVM has a Naimark dilation circuit, though never an exact one, and a prepended draw from 2T, the least group that suffices, twirls measurement-side noise to exactly depolarizing (a fixed approximation costs variance, never bias). Only the antipodal solids decompose into projective measurements, which excludes the tetrahedral SIC. There, one drawn rotation must both realize the POVM and twirl the noise: among groups, granted by 2T for all but the dodecahedron, which requires 2I.

title: Quantum Topology: An Intrinsic Information Encoding and Transfer Method
abstract: Quantum topology, a fascinating field of physics, offers the potential for novel information encoding and transmission methods. This paper explores the application of quantum topology to design a secure and efficient information transfer protocol. We propose a method leveraging the unique properties of quantum topology, specifically the formation of topological defects and the interplay of quantum entanglement, to achieve information security and enhanced transmission speeds. This research focuses on a novel approach that utilizes the inherent structure of quantum systems to create a robust and adaptable system for secure communication. The core mechanism involves exploiting topological properties to circumvent traditional cryptographic vulnerabilities. The paper details the theoretical underpinnings, proposes a practical implementation framework, and discusses the potential implications for future quantum information security.

title: 基于量子纠缠的复杂计算模型
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement as a novel computational paradigm to address the limitations of traditional computing models. We propose a new computational model predicated on the dynamic behavior of entangled quantum states, aiming to achieve precise modeling and simulation of complex systems. The core mechanism focuses on establishing a quantum entanglement-based dynamic simulation model, leveraging the inherent non-linear properties of entanglement to facilitate accurate computations. The research investigates the advantages of this approach, particularly the potential for automated parameter adjustment and reduced computational complexity compared to traditional methods. The paper details the theoretical framework underpinning this model and presents preliminary results demonstrating the feasibility of this approach in simulating specific complex systems.

title: DW-FMAL Wireless Interference Dataset
abstract: This dataset contains 800,000 simulated I/Q samples for cross-domain wireless interference recognition under domain shifts caused by transmitter devices, propagation channels, and interference-to-noise ratios. It covers 16 interference classes over a complete grid of 5 devices, 5 channel conditions, and 5 INR values, forming 125 domains. Each sample contains 512 complex-baseband sampling points represented by two float32 I/Q channels. The dataset supports the associated paper Cross-domain wireless interference recognition via dynamically weighted adversarial learning.
